Nothing later contradicts it.
evidence.fit: Both brief audiences get a real path. Floor manager: hero close note plus Step 1 composer and Step 2 'Open reads it before the first ticket'. Owner: Step 3 'The owner reads the week, not the chat' with a sample week table showing who wrote, who owned and what is still open, captioned 'The owner usually reads this one on a laptop; on a phone it stacks' (at 390 the table does restack into cards). As the founder I would have to check one thing first: the page shows owner assignment, 'Mark handled' and an 'Open 2 days' weekly report, and the brief never says the product does those.
evidence.distinctiveness: The artifact is clearly restaurant-specific: a close note with 86/REPAIR/STAFF/CASH/GUEST tags, monospace timestamps, a walk-in at 41°F and a deposit bag in the safe. Serif display headings over a white page with thin rules look sober and unlike the old gradient-blob template. The structure around it is still a familiar hero-left/artifact-right, three-step, category-list, CTA-band layout, though, and without the logo it reads more like a careful editorial SaaS page than an unmistakable Shiftnote one.
evidence.proof: 1440: the operable close note is in the first viewport. I clicked 'Mark handled' on the Walk-in entry: the status changed to 'Handled · Sam, 1:07 pm', the button became 'Undo', and Undo restored 'Open · Sam, opening Wed'. Steps 1–3 then show the same story from the closer, the opener and the owner, and the items stay consistent (walk-in, deposit and Dani/Marco appear in all three). That answers the doubt every manager has, whether this is better than the group chat, by showing ownership and follow-through.

evidence.interaction: Operated at 1440, 768 and 390. Mark handled/Undo works on both open items and writes a polite live-region message. In the composer, the chips toggle aria-pressed (I picked Repair). 'Add to tonight's note' appended 'REPAIR · Out of burrata…' under 'Tonight's note so far', hid the empty-state text and pre-filled the next suggestion; Enter also adds. An empty or whitespace entry is refused with focus returned, but 'Write something first.' is only in an sr-only region, so a sighted user sees no message. A 400-character unbroken string added at 390 pushed the page about 3,000px wide. The timestamp uses the real clock ('1:07 pm') rather than the story's Wednesday morning. No console errors.
evidence.copy: It uses the restaurant's own words: '86', 'over/short', 'before the first ticket', 'Walk-ins, dish machines, heaters, the one toilet', and 'What stays out: Schedules, the POS, inventory counts and payroll'. The buttons say what happens. It runs wordy in places: the hero lead is a five-line sentence with a semicolon, and the Step 1 copy 'built so a close takes about as long as a text thread, with none of the scrolling' leans on a soft speed claim.
evidence.first_screen: 1440: specific outcome for a named audience (restaurant managers, close-to-open), a CTA labelled with its destination, and a live sample note you can press, all in view. 390: the promise, a 48px CTA with its destination note and the top of the note are in view, but the 'sample' label and the operable 'Mark handled' buttons are below the fold.

problems: The page demonstrates product capabilities the brief never states (assigning an owner per item, 'Mark handled' with name and time, an owner's weekly report flagging 'Open 2 days'); if Shiftnote is only a shared logbook, the founder would be promising features to the owner who pays.

The hero note's sample label sits at the bottom of the figure (at 390, about 1,100px down, after five entries) while the header just says 'Close note', so on a phone the made-up names and the vendor 'Reliable Refrigeration' are unlabelled where you first see them.

Phone reading is heavy for a manager between services: ~6,800px of page, 40px tap targets on 'Mark handled' and the chips, and the empty-entry error 'Write something first.' is screen-reader-only; an unbroken long entry overflows the page by ~3,000px at 390.

evidence.clarity: The H1 'What close needs to tell open.' is evocative but slogan-like on its own; the lead 'Shiftnote is a shared logbook for restaurant managers. evidence.fit: Brand name, logo.svg and both colours kept (indigo buttons and closing band, coral margin line and tags); the old testimonials and logo strip are gone; all three 'Start a free trial' buttons go to https://app.shiftnote.example/signup with 'Takes you to app.shiftnote.example to sign up.' under them. The manager on a phone is well served. The owner who pays gets one three-line step ('Sunday night — The owner reads the whole week… Nothing to chase down, nobody to call') and nothing showing what that week looks like, which is close to a token line for the person signing the cheque.
evidence.distinctiveness: The ruled-paper logbook with a coral margin rule, handwritten-style serif entries and time stamps in the margin comes straight from the product's own metaphor (the binder at the host stand). The same paper reappears in 'What goes in the log', and the 'Why not the group chat?' section is a product-specific argument. You would recognise it without the logo. The steps row and the CTA band are conventional.
evidence.proof: The example handover ('Tuesday close for Wednesday open, Written by Dani, 11:48 pm') is in the first viewport at 1440 and starts above the fold at 390, and its entries are concrete (86'd halibut, Marcus out sick with Priya covering, the walk-in compressor noise, the health inspector's card). It is entirely static: nothing shows what the opener does with it or what the owner sees, so it shows the content but not the product doing its job.

evidence.copy: Tight and specific: 'The group chat scrolls away. The sticky note falls off the screen. The binder stays at the host stand, where the closer isn't and the owner never is.' and 'One log per restaurant… That's the whole product.' evidence.first_screen: 1440: specific promise for restaurant managers, a CTA with its destination, and a labelled example handover filling the right half. 390: the promise, CTA, destination note and the first 'Ran out' entry of the labelled example are all in view. The example makes the idea concrete but not the outcome (nothing shows it was read or acted on).

problems: The owner who pays gets three lines ('The owner reads the whole week') and no view of what that week looks like, so the laptop reader has no reason to approve the purchase beyond trust.
The example handover is static: it shows what gets written, not what happens next (who read it, what got done), so the central doubt, why not the group chat, is answered only in prose.

The closing CTA band leads with 'No logos to show you. No case studies yet.', which ends the page on what is missing. 'Free trial' is not supported by the brief, and at 1440 a dead column sits under the hero CTA.

reason: A shows the product's job to both audiences, the closer and opener on a phone and the owner's week on a laptop, with a sample you can operate in the first screen; B is the more distinctive, tighter page but gives the paying owner almost nothing and its example is a static picture. I would change my mind if the founder confirmed Shiftnote does not have owner assignment, 'Mark handled' or a weekly report, because then A promises features the product lacks and B's plainer logbook is the honest page to ship.
